title: Third Time's the Charm: Looking at Brains, Books, and Lesson Blueprints to Make Three-Cueing Make Sense
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos, a first and second grade reading interventionist, draws on a 2026 review of sixty years of three-cueing research by Maria Nicholas and Ondine Bradbury to explain why the system remains so confused and contentious. She argues the confusion comes from failing to separate what happens in the proficient reader's brain, what is on the page in a book, and what belongs in a lesson blueprint for beginners. Ken Goodman's hasty generalizations encouraged guessing, but the review shows the cues work as a self-monitoring mechanism rather than a way to teach decoding. Beginning readers cannot yet integrate the cues, so they need explicit fix-it steps: go for the graphemes, flex the phonemes, and confirm with context. She argues that using context to confirm a decoding attempt, rather than to guess, preserves orthographic mapping, and that cueing support should be released gradually.
points: Janetos locates the long confusion over three-cueing in a failure to distinguish the brain, the book and the lesson blueprint.
Nicholas and Bradbury's review reads the three cues as a self-monitoring mechanism, not a method for teaching children to decode.
Beginning readers lack the facility to integrate the cues the way proficient readers do, so they need isolated fix-it strategies at the point of failure.
Her classroom routine is to go for the graphemes, flex the phonemes, and confirm with context.
Using context to confirm rather than to identify a word protects orthographic mapping and long-term automatic recognition.
quotes: I believe it rests with failing to distinguish what’s happening in the brain, from what’s happening in the book, from what’s happening in the blueprint for a lesson.

I have tried to explain to my whole language correspondents that what happens in the proficient reader’s brain isn’t happening in the beginning reader’s brain yet simply because of this lack of proficiency with written language.
Just coming up with a word based on pictures or context—rather than using context to confirm her decoding effort—bypasses the opportunity for orthographic mapping and can stall word recognition.

Note that even a beginning reader can—must—monitor comprehension, such as when my student said mack instead of make, in order for a word to become orthographically mapped for future automatic recognition by uniting all three elements—phonology, orthography, and semantics.
We can’t pretend that these language processes don’t exist. But we also can’t pretend that there isn’t a logical approach to help students become aware of these processes.

Yes, we want them to attempt to identify a word by decoding it so that it can become orthographically mapped, but we also want them to confirm the chosen word by using context (syntax and semantics)—and we certainly do not want them to engage in context-based guessing.

This is a simple, straightforward process that I can offer my beginning readers, a system they will eventually use to self-monitor during independent reading and continue to use as proficient readers who inevitably encounter unknown words despite their overall skill level.
